answers.primary: Project memory: a CLAUDE.md at the repository root, committed to version control, holding the build command, the Postgres test prerequisite and the handler directory as short factual lines. It is auto-loaded into every session for everyone who clones the repo, which is exactly the always-on shared-baseline shape.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill, rejected because a skill is loaded only when the model judges its description relevant, so these orientation facts would be absent from the sessions that need them most (the first minutes of a fresh session).
answers.enforcement_owner: Shared between the two but effectively the model. The harness owns loading the file into context deterministically; the model owns whether it actually uses the facts, and nothing checks that it did.
answers.context_boundary: The main session context window. The full file text crosses in at session start and stays resident for the whole session, so it is charged on every request and it is what compaction may summarize away.
answers.lifecycle: Runs at session start in any session rooted in that repo, refreshes when the file is edited and re-read, and stops applying when the file is deleted or when the session moves outside the repo. It has no per-task trigger.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and is purely advisory: the model can and does drift from it, and drift gets worse as the file grows and after context compaction. The realistic decay path is scope creep, the file becomes a wiki, the signal-to-noise ratio drops, and adherence falls.
answers.version_caveat: Root CLAUDE.md project memory is one of the oldest and most stable Claude Code mechanisms, so no version gate, plan restriction or enabling flag applies in practice. The only moving parts I would verify against the installed version are the import syntax for pulling in other files and the deprecation status of CLAUDE.local.md; I cannot state those precisely without the documentation.

answers.primary: A skill: a directory under .claude/skills/ with a SKILL.md whose description names release-note generation, the 30 steps in the body, and the template plus the changelog query script as bundled files the skill points at. Progressive disclosure is the whole point: only the frontmatter sits in context until the weekly task actually comes up.
answers.rejected_alternative: A custom slash command, rejected because the procedure is long enough that a single expanded command body is unwieldy, and it cannot carry a script and a template as separate files the way a skill directory can.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. It decides the skill is relevant, decides to read the bundled files, and decides whether to follow all 30 steps in order; the harness only makes the skill discoverable.
answers.context_boundary: The main session context. Only the skill name and description are resident by default; the SKILL.md body enters context on invocation, and the template and script contents only enter if the model reads or executes them.
answers.lifecycle: Triggered when the model matches the description to a release-notes request (or when the user names it), and it stops applying once that task is finished. Nothing keeps it loaded between weekly runs.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open in two distinct ways: the skill may never trigger because the request was phrased in words the description does not cover, or it triggers and the model quietly compresses a 30-step procedure into the ten steps it considers important. Long linear procedures are exactly where step-skipping shows up, so the steps that produce a checkable artifact should be script calls rather than prose instructions.
answers.version_caveat: Agent Skills are a comparatively recent addition to Claude Code and require a reasonably current version; I cannot give the exact minimum version or a flag name from memory. Worth confirming against the installed build whether skills live under .claude/skills/ with the frontmatter fields you expect, and whether skills in your version are also invocable by name.

answers.primary: A custom slash command: a markdown file under .claude/commands/ (for example /reseed-staging) whose body is the encoded procedure, invoked only by an explicit user keystroke. User-invoked-only is the structural property the requirement is asking for, and it is what separates this from every model-invoked mechanism.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill, rejected precisely because skills are model-invoked from a description match, so a conversation that merely looks staging-adjacent could cause the assistant to decide a reseed is warranted.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the trigger: the command body simply does not enter the conversation unless the user types the command. The model still owns execution of the steps once it is invoked.
answers.context_boundary: The main session context. The command file is expanded into the current turn's prompt at invocation time, along with any arguments, and nothing else crosses.
answers.lifecycle: Runs on the explicit user invocation, applies for the turn or task that follows, and stops applying when that work completes. It has no ambient presence between invocations.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed on the autonomous-trigger requirement, which is the requirement that matters here, but fails open on execution: the body is still prose the model interprets, so it may reorder or skip a step. Note the command does not gate the destructive action itself, so if you also want to stop an ad-hoc drop issued outside the command, that needs a PreToolUse hook or a permissions deny rule on the drop/reseed command shape.
answers.version_caveat: Custom slash commands from .claude/commands/ are long-standing and unrestricted by plan. The caveat is version drift in the other direction: in some versions skills are also reachable as slash-style invocations and appear in the menu, so verify on the installed version that what you shipped is a command and not something the model can also self-trigger.

answers.primary: A path-scoped instruction file: a nested CLAUDE.md placed at src/api/CLAUDE.md carrying the three conventions, leaving the root file untouched. Subtree memory loads when Claude works on files under that directory, so the conventions are present exactly when they matter and cost nothing in sessions that never touch the API package.
answers.rejected_alternative: Appending the conventions to the root CLAUDE.md, rejected because that file is already at its useful size limit and adding always-on text is what caused adherence to slip in the first place.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. Loading is harness-driven but conditional on the model touching that subtree, and compliance with all three conventions is entirely the model's choice; nothing rejects an endpoint that lacks the error envelope.
answers.context_boundary: The main session context, entered partway through the session rather than at start. Only the nested file's text crosses, and only once work reaches that directory.
answers.lifecycle: Loads when the session reads or edits files under src/api/, remains for the rest of that session once loaded, and never loads in sessions confined to other packages. It stops applying when the file is removed or the code moves out of that path.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open, and the specific hazard is a load gap: if the model writes a new handler by path without first reading anything in that subtree, the nested file may never be pulled in and the conventions are silently absent. If the conventions are genuinely non-negotiable, back the file with a PostToolUse lint hook or a CI check, since the instruction file alone cannot guarantee an OpenAPI comment exists.
answers.version_caveat: Nested per-directory CLAUDE.md files are a long-standing feature, but the exact load semantics (eager discovery of all nested files versus on-demand load when a file in that directory is touched) have differed across versions, so verify the behavior on the installed build. If your version supports glob-scoped rule files with frontmatter path patterns, that is a tighter fit than a nested memory file, but I cannot confirm from memory that this repo's Claude Code version has that.

answers.primary: User-level memory: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md on that engineer's machine, holding the indentation preference, the commit-message convention and the diff-review flow, paired with their personal ~/.claude/settings.json for anything that is configuration rather than instruction. User scope is per-machine and per-person by construction, so nothing reaches teammates.
answers.rejected_alternative: A project CLAUDE.md, rejected because it is committed and would impose one engineer's personal habits on the whole team through the shared repo, which is exactly the outcome the request excludes.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The harness reliably loads the user memory file, but every item in it is a preference the model applies at its discretion.
answers.context_boundary: Every session's main context window on that machine, in every repository they open. The file text crosses in at session start; nothing crosses into the repository or into a teammate's session.
answers.lifecycle: Applies from session start in all projects on that machine, for as long as the file exists, and stops when it is edited or the engineer works on a different machine. It is not tied to any task or trigger.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and advisory, plus a precedence trap: when a personal preference collides with a project convention or a repository formatter config, project-scope instructions and the actual tooling win, so a 2-space preference will be silently overwritten by the repo's formatter. It also drifts as the file accumulates preferences nobody prunes.
answers.version_caveat: User-scope ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is stable and requires no flag or plan. I would verify the current status of CLAUDE.local.md and of the import syntax against the installed version rather than trusting recall, since I believe the local-file variant has been superseded by imports but cannot state that with confidence.

answers.primary: A hook pair around a version-controlled memory file: a SessionEnd (or Stop) hook running a script that distills the session's confirmed corrections into appended entries, and a SessionStart hook that injects the accumulated file back into the new session. The accumulation is the harness's job precisely because nobody will do it by hand.
answers.rejected_alternative: The interactive memory shortcut for adding a line to CLAUDE.md by hand, rejected because it depends on a human remembering to capture at the moment of learning, which is the behavior the team has already said will not happen.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns that capture fires at all and that the accumulated file is injected. The model owns what gets written, which is the weak half: it decides which corrections were real lessons.
answers.context_boundary: Two boundaries. The capture script runs outside the model's context in its own process, and only the distilled entries it writes persist; on the next session, only that distilled file crosses into the fresh context window, never the previous transcript.
answers.lifecycle: Capture fires on the session-end (or stop) event of every session in that repository; injection fires at the start of every subsequent session. Entries persist indefinitely, so the lifecycle only ends if something prunes them.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and it is the accumulation itself that rots: the file grows without bound, stale entries (a test that is no longer flaky, a container that was replaced) keep getting injected, and one wrongly captured lesson poisons every later session. A hook that errors loses its capture silently, so treat the file as needing periodic review and a size or recency cap rather than as self-maintaining.
answers.version_caveat: Session-lifecycle hook events (SessionStart, SessionEnd) were added later than the PreToolUse and PostToolUse events, so this design has a real minimum-version dependency, and I cannot name the version or the exact event names with confidence from memory. Verify both the available event names and the mechanism for a hook to inject text into the context on the installed build; an MCP memory server is the alternative implementation if those events are not available.

answers.primary: A custom output style, selected for that group's environment. Output styles change the system prompt itself rather than appending to it, so a non-default style is the only mechanism that both installs the runbook voice and structure and removes the built-in software-engineering framing that keeps pulling answers toward code.
answers.rejected_alternative: A CLAUDE.md persona instruction, rejected because CLAUDE.md is additive: it can ask for a calm runbook voice but it cannot delete the built-in coding-oriented behavior underneath, so the pull toward code changes would persist.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns which system prompt is in force. The model owns whether it holds the voice and the fixed structure in every response, so tone consistency itself is unenforced.
answers.context_boundary: The system prompt of every session in that configuration, ahead of all conversation content. It applies to all output in the session; nothing crosses back out.
answers.lifecycle: Applies from the moment the style is selected, persists across sessions once saved in settings, and stops when the style is switched back to default or removed. It is not per-task.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open on adherence, and the removal itself carries a cost: stripping the engineering instructions also removes behavior around tool use and code-adjacent tasks, so if this group ever needs a file edited or a log parsed, quality drops. Structure drift over a long incident thread is the common practical complaint.
answers.version_caveat: Output styles are a comparatively recent feature and I believe their status has shifted since introduction (deprecation or absorption into another mechanism has been discussed), so this is the field I am least confident about. Confirm on the installed version that custom output styles still exist and where they are stored before committing a support-ops workflow to them; if they do not, the fallback is a dedicated system-prompt override at the Agent SDK or launcher level.

answers.primary: A PreToolUse hook matched on Bash (and on any git-capable MCP tool) that parses the command and returns a deny decision for any push targeting the protected branch. A hook is code the harness runs before the tool call, so the outcome does not depend on the model having read or remembered anything.
answers.rejected_alternative: A more strongly worded CLAUDE.md instruction, rejected on evidence: it has already failed twice, and the post-compaction failure is the proof that instruction text is a context-resident artifact rather than a guarantee.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness, unambiguously. This is the whole reason to pick a hook: the decision is made outside the model, and the model cannot argue with it or forget it.
answers.context_boundary: The hook executes in its own process outside the model's context window, receiving the tool input as JSON. Only the decision and the message it prints cross back into the transcript, which is also how the model learns why it was blocked.
answers.lifecycle: Fires before every matching tool invocation for the entire session, including after compaction and including in subagent contexts, and stops applying only if the hook configuration is removed or the file is made non-executable.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed on the shapes it matches, but the realistic breach is coverage, not bypassed logic: aliases, git -C, a push buried in a shell chain or in a script the model executes, a force push through a different remote name, or a git MCP server that never touches Bash. A malformed hook or a nonzero exit that the harness treats as an error rather than a denial can also fail open, so pair the hook with server-side branch protection, which is the only guarantee that survives someone bypassing Claude Code entirely.
answers.version_caveat: Hook configuration has moved across versions: the decision protocol (a blocking exit code versus a structured JSON permission decision field) and the exact set of hook event names changed as hooks matured, so write the hook against the installed version's schema rather than from recall, since I cannot state the field names or exit-code semantics with certainty. Also check whether the permissions deny list in settings can express the same rule on your version, which is a simpler belt to add alongside the braces.

answers.primary: A skill whose description names the billing engine and its topics, with the long explainer split so that SKILL.md is a short orienting body and the states, invariants and traps live in bundled reference files the skill points to. This is the reference-material shape: model-invoked on topic match, and nearly free when billing does not come up.
answers.rejected_alternative: A custom slash command, rejected on two counts: it would appear in the command menu, which the request excludes, and it would only ever load when a human explicitly asked, whereas this should arrive whenever billing surfaces in conversation.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. It decides from the description that billing is in play and decides how much of the reference to read; nothing in the harness makes it consult the explainer before answering a billing question.
answers.context_boundary: The main session context. Only name and description are resident up front; the SKILL.md body enters on trigger and each reference file only when explicitly read, which is what keeps a long document off the per-request bill.
answers.lifecycle: Triggers when the conversation matches the description, stays in context for the remainder of the session once loaded, and may be dropped at compaction, after which a later billing question can silently run without it.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open, with under-triggering as the characteristic failure: the model answers a billing question from its own priors and never notices the skill exists, especially if the question uses domain words the description does not contain. Over-broad descriptions produce the opposite problem, loading a long document into unrelated sessions, so the description wording is the real tuning surface.
answers.version_caveat: This depends on Agent Skills being present and on the version's progressive-disclosure behavior for bundled files; I cannot give the minimum version or confirm the frontmatter field set from memory. One thing to check explicitly on the installed build is whether skills also surface in the slash-command menu, since the requirement says this must not appear there, and that visibility behavior has varied.

answers.primary: Enterprise managed policy settings deployed by MDM (the managed-settings.json administered at the machine-wide policy path, for example under ProgramData on Windows or the system-level application-support path on macOS and Linux), pointing at an admin-owned instruction file or a SessionStart hook that injects the reminders. Managed policy is the only scope that user and project settings cannot override, which is what makes opt-out impossible.
answers.rejected_alternative: A user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md rolled out by script, rejected because it lives in a location developers own and can edit or delete, so the no-opt-out requirement fails the first time someone finds it inconvenient.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns loading: the policy is applied regardless of what the developer configures. The model still owns whether the data-handling reminders are actually followed, so the guarantee is about presence, not compliance.
answers.context_boundary: Every session on every managed machine and every repository, at session start. The reminder text crosses into each session's context window and is charged on every request, so the text must be short.
answers.lifecycle: Applies at session start for as long as the MDM policy is in place, updates when the policy is redeployed, and stops only when the security organization changes or withdraws it. Developers have no lifecycle control over it.
answers.failure_mode: Loading fails closed, adherence fails open: the reminders always arrive but remain advisory prose the model can drift from, particularly after compaction on a long session. Two practical hazards are that a policy file that is malformed or at the wrong path silently does nothing (so verify on a representative machine rather than assuming), and that always-on text on every session is the most expensive place to put anything, which pushes toward a few lines of policy plus hooks for the rules that must actually be enforced.
answers.version_caveat: Managed settings and their precedence over user and project settings are an enterprise-oriented feature whose file paths, supported keys and version requirement I cannot state exactly from memory, and whether hooks declared in managed settings are honored is specifically worth verifying. Confirm the path and the supported schema for the installed version and for each operating system in the fleet before relying on it; there may also be a plan or deployment-tier condition attached.
